title: The paper's one novel force is an assumption, not a result: verification is imposed to be length-independent and perfectly informative, and the theory collapses to a known batching/inspection problem once it is relaxed
location: 3_shortrun.tex Sec 3.2 (Definition 3, chain cost $\AItime{r}/\prod_{i=\ell}^r q_i$); 1_introduction.tex l.85-88; 4_implications.tex eq (2)
claim: The entire paper rests on one modelling choice stated as a definition and never examined: "Managing one attempt at the chain therefore costs the same as augmenting step $s_r$, namely time $\AItime{r}$ per attempt" (3_shortrun.tex Sec 3.2), and the intro's plain-English version, "verifying a report produced after AI executes Steps~3--4 takes the same effort as verifying one produced after AI executes Step 4 alone; the AI is just less likely to succeed at the former" (1_introduction.tex l.88). Four things are simultaneously assumed here and none is discussed anywhere in 131 pages: (a) the human's verification cost does not rise with chain length; (b) automated steps cost zero human time AND zero AI/compute cost (defended only in a footnote appealing to "the AI subscription business model"); (c) failure of the chain is detected perfectly and at zero cost at the endpoint, so the retry structure $\AItime{r}/\prod q_i$ is exact; (d) a failed chain is re-run in its entirety for the same $\AItime{r}$. Given (a)-(d), every headline result is immediate arithmetic: a fixed cost shared over a contiguous block makes blocks cheap, so blocks form, so block-membership beats own-characteristics, so thresholds appear. There is no economic force here beyond "indivisible fixed cost spread over adjacent units." The economically interesting case is precisely the one assumed away. If the human only imperfectly detects a bad chain output -- which is the whole reason AI oversight is a live problem -- then expected quality loss rises with the number of unverified intermediate steps, verification becomes a marginal rather than a fixed cost, and the sign of eq (2) can flip. Likewise if $\AItime{r}$ is replaced by anything increasing in $r-\ell$, the chaining force is bounded and the comparative-advantage overturning may vanish. The paper never states which of its results survive any perturbation of (a)-(d).
why_it_matters: The paper is sold as a theory paper whose contribution is a new economic force ("verification is a fixed cost of the chain rather than a marginal cost that scales with its length"). If that is a primitive assumption rather than something derived from a verification technology, and if it is knife-edge, then Propositions 1 and 2, the non-monotonicity result, and the entire empirical agenda inherit the assumption rather than testing it. A ReStud referee asked "is this a genuinely new economic force or a relabelling?" will conclude: relabelling. Everything in Sections 3-4 is the classical problem of where to place inspection stations in a serial production line with stage-specific defect probabilities -- a solved operations problem with exactly this DP -- with 'inspection' renamed 'verification' and 'defect rate' renamed 'AI difficulty'.
already_addressed: Nothing found. `grep -rin "verif" *.tex` returns 20 hits, all of which assert the fixed-cost property; none questions it. There is no robustness section, no extension, and no footnote on length-dependent verification cost, imperfect error detection, or per-token/per-call AI cost. The only related caveat is the footnote in 3_shortrun.tex Sec 3.2 claiming "The main forces discussed in the model remain at play even if we assume each time the firm deploys AI on a step it has to incur a cost. We deliberately avoid modeling this to prevent complicating the model." That is an unproven assertion about a different assumption (marginal AI cost), and it does not touch (a), (c), or (d).
fix: Two things are needed. First, microfound verification: let the human choose a verification intensity and let detection probability of an upstream error decay in the number of unverified steps, so that $\AItime{}$ for a chain over $\ell..r$ becomes $v(r-\ell)$ with $v'>0$, plus an expected cost of passing a bad output downstream. Then state the exact condition on $v$ under which the chaining force survives -- e.g. show that overturning of comparative advantage obtains iff $v$ grows more slowly than the retry-inflation factor $1/\prod q_i$. That converts the paper's engine from an assumption into a theorem with a testable boundary. Second, add a proposition characterizing what happens as the automated step's direct AI cost $c>0$ rises from zero, and show the chaining region shrinks continuously rather than discontinuously. Without at least one of these, the theory section is a worked example of fixed-cost batching.

title: The empirics pool automation with augmentation, so they test a prediction the model shares with the standard task-based model; the one test of the model's distinguishing mode is insignificant and is buried in the appendix
location: 7_empirics.tex l.28 and Secs 7.1-7.3; D_tables_and_robustness.tex Sec D.3 (l.131-135); 4_implications.tex l.186
claim: Section 7 states: "We therefore do not distinguish the two labels in what follows and treat both as indicating AI execution" (7_empirics.tex l.28). But 'automated' is the only mode in the model that requires a chain -- augmentation is a length-one chain, i.e. a human prompting and verifying a single step, which is exactly the standard task-level substitution the paper says it departs from. Once the two are pooled, all three predictions are predictions about *whether a step is AI-executed*, and the model's own worked example says clustering need not change that: "The same two steps are executed by AI either way, since an isolated easy step is already worth augmenting on its own; what the arrangement changes is what that AI execution costs" (4_implications.tex l.186). The paper's escape hatch is the very next sentence -- "Where an isolated exposed step is \emph{not} worth augmenting on its own, a case the model equally permits, dispersion suppresses AI execution outright" -- but that parameter region is never characterized, never argued to be the empirically relevant one, and never used to sign the predicted magnitudes. Meanwhile the headline statistic is a mean observed chain length of 1.45 (Sec 7.1), and under the paper's own length-one convention a chain of length 1 contains zero automated steps; a mean of 1.45 therefore says the modal AI-executed step in the data involves no automation at all. Finally, when the authors do run the model's distinguishing test, replacing $\text{is\_ai}_t$ with $\text{is\_automated}_t$, they report in the appendix: "Under this stricter specification, the estimated effects are smaller in magnitude and often statistically insignificant" (D_tables_and_robustness.tex l.135).
why_it_matters: The abstract's third contribution -- "Empirical evidence supports the model's key predictions" -- does not survive. What the data support is that AI-exposed and AI-used tasks cluster in an LLM-imputed ordering, which a plain Acemoglu-Restrepo model with spatially correlated task characteristics predicts equally well. The chaining mechanism, which is the paper's claimed novelty, is tested exactly once (the is_automated regressions) and fails to reject the null. That is the sentence a referee will quote back. It also means the paper's answer to 'is this one paper or two?' is that the empirical paper is testing a different model from the theoretical one.
already_addressed: Partially, and the paper's own handling makes it worse rather than better. C_sample_construction.tex Sec C.1 (l.177-184) documents the discrepancy honestly -- automated tasks are sometimes followed by manual ones because "the Anthropic classifications are based on task-level feasibility and are agnostic to workflow position" -- and uses that as the justification for pooling. D_tables_and_robustness.tex Sec D.3 runs the is_automated version and reports it as a robustness check whose weakness "reflect[s] the more limited prevalence of AI automation in the data." What is missing: any acknowledgement that pooling removes the model's distinguishing content, any statement of what the pooled prediction is that the standard model does *not* also make, and any power calculation showing whether the is_automated test could have detected the effect it failed to find.
fix: Promote the automation-only test to the main text and treat it as the paper's central empirical result, with an explicit power analysis (given the automated-label base rate, what effect size would the DWA-FE specification detect at 80% power?). Separately, derive the sharp prediction the pooled model does *not* deliver: from eq (2), the marginal cost of folding step $k$ in depends on $\AItime{k+1}(1-q_k)/(q_kq_{k+1})$, so among *unexposed* steps the neighbor effect should be strictly positive and increasing in neighbor reliability, while among steps already worth augmenting alone it should be zero. Test that heterogeneity: a neighbor effect concentrated on E0/unexposed focal steps is evidence of chaining; a uniform effect is evidence of correlated comparative advantage. That is the one design in this dataset that separates the two models.

title: Every empirical prediction is also implied by a plain comparative-advantage model in which adjacent steps in a workflow are similar; the paper never states or tests that null
location: 7_empirics.tex Secs 7.1-7.3, eq (5) and eq (6); D_tables_and_robustness.tex Sec D.3
claim: Consider the alternative model the paper is trying to beat: tasks have independent AI-ability, exactly as in Acemoglu-Restrepo, but adjacent steps in a workflow are similar in modality (write, then edit, then format; measure, then adjust, then re-measure). Then (i) AI-executed steps cluster, because AI-able steps cluster -- Prediction 1; (ii) occupations whose AI-able steps are dispersed have fewer AI-executed steps, because dispersion is a proxy for how heterogeneous the workflow's modalities are and hence for how many exposed steps clear the threshold -- Prediction 2; (iii) a step is more likely to be AI-executed when its neighbors are, because its neighbors' execution proxies for its own unobserved within-DWA AI-ability -- Prediction 3. The paper's placebos do not touch this null. The position reshuffles in Sec 7.1 and Fig 4 destroy the correlation between adjacency and similarity, so they reject 'ordering is pure noise' and nothing more; the paper concedes as much ("these tests rule out either input being pure noise") but then does not confront what the tests do not rule out. In eq (6) the controls are "the step $t$'s AI exposure status and number of steps in the occupation" -- the neighbors' *exposure* status is never controlled for anywhere in the draft (`grep -rn "prev.*exposed\|neighbor.*exposure" *.tex` returns nothing). Since $\text{prev\_is\_ai}$ is a deterministic function of prev's exposure and prev's own characteristics, and exposure is spatially correlated, $\beta_2$ in eq (6) is a within-DWA proxy for the focal step's residual AI-ability.
why_it_matters: The empirical section's stated purpose is to establish that "AI execution depends not only on comparative advantage and step-level characteristics, but also on the local work context" (1_introduction.tex, Empirical Evidence). If the estimates are equally consistent with comparative advantage plus spatially correlated characteristics, the empirical contribution over the existing exposure-measurement literature (Felten, Webb, Eloundou) is zero, and Section 7 becomes a descriptive appendix rather than a test.
already_addressed: Partially. DWA fixed effects (col 4 of Table 6) absorb between-activity differences in AI-ability, and Appendix D.3 tightens 'similar' using a GPT similarity filter within DWA. Appendices F and G rule out prompt artefacts and O*NET filler tasks, and Appendix H validates the LLM ordering against APQC and 4TU logs. None of these addresses the confound, because all of them concern whether the *ordering* is real, not whether adjacency proxies for similarity. DWA FE removes the between-DWA component of AI-ability but leaves the within-DWA, within-occupation component, which is exactly the component correlated with neighbors' execution.
fix: Add neighbors' exposure ($\text{prev\_is\_exposed}$, $\text{next\_is\_exposed}$, and their E1/E2 split) to eq (6) alongside neighbors' execution. The chaining mechanism predicts that neighbors' *execution* retains explanatory power conditional on neighbors' *exposure* -- exposure is the step-characteristic channel, execution is the chaining channel. If the execution coefficients survive that horse race, the paper has identified something the standard model cannot produce; if they do not, the finding is comparative advantage with correlated characteristics. This is a one-line change to a regression the authors already run, and it is the single most valuable exercise in the paper.

title: The abstract claims a characterization the paper explicitly concedes it does not have; Proposition 1 is three numerical examples plus continuity, and holds only with the rest of the workflow frozen
location: 0_main.tex l.69 (abstract); 4_implications.tex l.122 and l.130; A_omitted_proofs.tex Sec A.1, proof of part (i)
claim: The abstract asserts: "We characterize how a firm optimally assigns humans and AI across the steps of its workflow, and show that AI chaining can overturn comparative advantage logic" (0_main.tex l.69). Two sentences in the body retract both halves. On characterization: "Even though characterizing the execution mode of each individual step in the optimal arrangement is hard..." (4_implications.tex l.130). On overturning: "We must note that Proposition~\ref{prop:ca_local} is a \emph{local} statement: it compares rearrangements of a step and its neighbors while holding the AI strategy on the rest of the workflow fixed, and so they fall short of determining whether the overturning takes place in the cost-minimizing arrangement of the entire production sequence" (4_implications.tex l.122). Proposition 1's hypotheses are even narrower than that sentence admits: the block $\{k-1,k,k+1\}$ is held fixed *and* "no chain [may] cross the block's boundary," which rules out precisely the global rearrangements that would determine the answer. And the proof of part (i) is not a general argument -- it sets $\manualTime{k-1}=\AItime{k-1}=\mu$, $\manualTime{k+1}=1$, $\AItime{k+1}=\tau$, exhibits three specific $(\mu,\tau)$ configurations, and invokes continuity to get an open neighbourhood. That is 'here are three examples, and they are not knife-edge.' Part (ii) is an upward-closedness (Topkis-style monotone comparative statics) result. The paper's flagship theoretical claim is therefore: an example, plus a monotonicity.
why_it_matters: ReStud's bar for a theory-leaning paper is a general result. What is on offer is a non-emptiness statement about an open set of parameters in a three-step block with the rest of the workflow frozen. An editor comparing the abstract's promise to Proposition 1 will read the gap as over-claiming, and a referee will ask the obvious question the paper leaves open -- does the overturning survive in the global optimum, and for what fraction of workflows? -- to which the paper has no answer.
already_addressed: The body is honest about the limitation in the two sentences quoted above, and Section 6.2 provides DP algorithms that compute the global optimum numerically. But honesty in the body does not fix an abstract that promises characterization, and a DP that computes an optimum is not a characterization of it. There is no global proposition anywhere: `grep -n "begin{proposition}" *.tex A_*.tex` yields exactly four, none of them global comparative statics.
fix: Either prove a global version -- e.g. in the optimal strategy for the full sequence, step $k$ is AI-executed whenever there exists an interval $[\ell,r]\ni k$ with $\AItime{r}/\prod_{i=\ell}^r q_i < \sum_{i=\ell}^r \minTime{i}$, giving a checkable sufficient condition on the whole workflow -- or use the $O(m^2)$ DP of Proposition 3 to characterize the optimum computationally: simulate workflows from a parameterized distribution of $(m_i,a_i,d_i)$ and report the share of human-advantaged steps that are AI-executed at the global optimum, as a function of $\alpha$ and of the autocorrelation of $d_i$ along the sequence. That second route also delivers the model-implied magnitude for Prediction 3, which the paper currently says it cannot benchmark ("we do not have a benchmark for what constitutes a large versus small effect in our context"). Regardless, rewrite the abstract to say 'we show' rather than 'we characterize', and to flag the result as local.

title: Proposition 2's fragmentation index and the empirical fragmentation index of Section 7.2 are different objects, so the paper's only theory-to-data bridge does not carry weight
location: 4_implications.tex Sec 4.2, eq (3) and Proposition 2; 7_empirics.tex Sec 7.2 (EFI definition, "a slightly modified metric")
claim: The theoretical fragmentation index is the expectation of $\sum_{i \in F}\min\{\manualTime{i}, \AItime{i}/q_i\} + \sum_{C_j \in \mathcal{C}} \omega(C_j)$ over the random set $F$ of steps at which AI fails, with $\omega(C_j)=\min\{1,\sum_{i\in C_j}\manualTime{i}\}$, and it is defined only under the normalization $\AItime{i}=1$ for all $i$. The empirical fragmentation index is "the ratio of the number of \emph{potential} tasks in the sense of our theoretical framework to the total number of steps," computed by "treat[ing] all AI-exposed tasks as identical for the purpose of potential chaining and assum[ing] that all of them could, in principle, be executed by AI" (7_empirics.tex Sec 7.2). The EFI therefore contains no $q_i$, no $\manualTime{i}$, no $\AItime{i}$, no expectation over failures, and no weights $\omega$ -- it is a deterministic count of maximal runs of E1/E2 steps divided by $m$. The paper describes the gap as "a slightly modified metric." It is a different statistic, and no result in the paper relates it to $OPT$. Compounding this: Proposition 2's guarantee is $\tfrac18 OPT \le FI \le \tfrac54 OPT$ (or $\tfrac14$ under $\manualTime{i}\ge1$). A factor-of-eight sandwich is a computer-science approximation guarantee, not an economic magnitude; it is consistent with $FI$ varying by 800% while $OPT$ is constant, so even for the genuine $FI$ the proposition does not sign $\partial OPT/\partial FI$ and cannot license the predicted sign of $\beta_2$ in eq (5). The normalization $\AItime{i}=1$ also switches off one of the two chaining forces the paper emphasizes -- the search for a "cheap verification endpoint" (1_introduction.tex l.91) requires heterogeneous $\AItime{i}$.
why_it_matters: Prediction 2 is the paper's clearest claim to have produced a *new measurement object* that improves on linear exposure indices -- the literature section sells fragmentation as "a bridge between occupation-level exposure measures and the actual patterns of AI execution." If the object tested is not the object theorized, and if the theorem about the theorized object is too loose to sign anything anyway, then the bridge is rhetorical. The negative $\beta_2$ then has no structural interpretation; it is a reduced-form fact about run-length in an LLM-imputed sequence.
already_addressed: The paper flags the substitution once ("we will make use of a slightly modified metric") and explains the omission of cost heterogeneity by data limitations ("we abstract from heterogeneity in tasks' underlying cost profiles, which are unobserved in our data"). Appendix D.2 adds EFI Definition 2 built from realized execution rather than exposure, with the correct caveat that it is mechanically related to the dependent variable. Nothing anywhere shows that either EFI is monotonically related to the theoretical $FI$, or that $FI$ within a factor of 8 of $OPT$ implies anything about the sign of a regression coefficient.
fix: Prove the missing link, or make it numeric. The cheapest credible version: take the DP of Proposition 3, simulate workflows with $q_i$ drawn from a distribution calibrated to the E1/E2 shares in O*NET, compute the true $OPT$, the true $FI$, and the EFI for each simulated workflow, and report (a) the correlation between EFI and $FI$, and (b) the regression of the model-implied AI-execution share on EFI conditional on exposure share and $\#$ AI-able steps -- i.e. run eq (5) on model-generated data. If that regression reproduces a negative $\beta_2$ of comparable magnitude, the empirical coefficient acquires a structural reading and the paper gains a quantitative test rather than a sign test. Separately, either tighten Proposition 2's constants or state plainly that the proposition establishes only that $FI$ is a valid order-of-magnitude summary, not a comparative statics tool.

title: The model cannot generate a J-curve: optimal cost is non-increasing in AI quality everywhere, by the paper's own proof, yet the intro and conclusion claim a microfoundation for it
location: 1_introduction.tex l.109; 8_conclusion.tex l.11; 2_literature.tex (Technology Adoption paragraph); A_omitted_proofs.tex Sec A.3, Lemma OA-3 and its proof
claim: The paper claims the J-curve three times. Intro: "Our framework thus provides a microfoundation for the productivity J-curve phenomenon \citep{brynjolfsson2021productivity}" (l.109). Conclusion: "it is consistent with the J-curve pattern of technology adoption, in which early adoption raises costs before the anticipated gains from reorganization are realized" (8_conclusion.tex l.11). Literature: it invokes \citet{mcelheran2025rise}, "which show that AI adoption initially reduces productivity." But the proof of Lemma OA-3 establishes $C_\T'(\alpha) = -\sum_c \AItime{r_c}D_c\alpha^{-D_c-1} \le 0$ for every strategy $\T$, so $C^*(\alpha)=\min_\T C_\T(\alpha)$, a minimum of non-increasing functions, is non-increasing on all of $(0,1]$. The model contains no adoption cost, no learning period, no transitional investment, and no state variable: automated steps are free, chains re-form instantaneously, and the firm re-optimizes costlessly at every $\alpha$. Productivity in this model never falls. What Lemma OA-3 delivers is an upward jump in the *derivative* $g^*=-\mathrm{d}C^*/\mathrm{d}\alpha$ at strategy switches -- and that is simply the statement that the lower envelope of a finite family of smooth convex decreasing curves has kinks, which is true in any model with discrete technology choice, including a discrete-automation Acemoglu-Restrepo. (The jump is also only weak: $\phi'(\alpha_0)\le 0$ gives $g_\T(\alpha_0)\le g_{\T'}(\alpha_0)$, so 'non-monotone' is not strictly established.)
why_it_matters: Non-monotonicity is one of the abstract's three advertised implications and the paper's main link to the macro/productivity-puzzle literature; it is also the mechanism the conclusion uses to "help explain why firms invest so heavily in AI capabilities even when short-run returns appear limited." If the result is (a) an envelope kink common to every discrete-choice model and (b) not a J-curve at all, then the paper's connection to Brynjolfsson-Rock-Syverson and to McElheran et al. is unearned, and a third of the abstract's contribution evaporates. A referee will note that the model predicts the opposite of the McElheran finding it cites as support.
already_addressed: Nothing found. Appendix A.3 is the formal treatment and it proves only what is described above; there is no intangible-investment stage, no adjustment cost, and no dynamic. Section 4.3 correctly describes the result as a jump in marginal returns, but the framing sentences in the introduction, literature review, and conclusion all slide from 'marginal returns jump' to 'costs rise first, then fall'.
fix: Either build the J-curve or drop the claim. Building it is cheap and would be a genuine contribution: add a one-time reorganization cost $\kappa$ that the firm pays when it switches strategy (retraining, re-engineering the workflow, rebuilding the hand-off interfaces), and note that $\kappa$ is naturally increasing in how far the new strategy's job design departs from the old. Then measured cost jumps *up* by $\kappa$ at each reorganization threshold before falling along the new envelope -- an actual J, with the depth of the J determined by the length of the chain being formed, which is a new and testable comparative static. Absent that, delete the J-curve sentences from l.109, 8_conclusion.tex l.11, and the literature review, and state the non-monotonicity result for what it is, noting explicitly that it is shared with any discrete-technology-choice model so that the reader is not misled about its novelty.

title: The abstract's CES aggregation claim is a reverse-engineered existence result that owes nothing to chaining
location: 0_main.tex l.72 (abstract); 6_extensions.tex Sec 6.1, eq (10) and its footnote; B_macro_production.tex l.163, l.211, l.218
claim: The abstract's closing sentence: "we... show that firm-level production aggregates to a macroeconomic CES production function" (0_main.tex l.72). Appendix B says what is actually done. Line 163: "This requires either determining the macro production function parameters from the distribution of heterogeneity, or specifying the form of heterogeneity given a set of macro production function parameters." Line 211: "Solving for $\phi(\bar{\alpha})$ in terms of $\theta_A,\theta_M,\rho$ we get the following distribution for effective AI quality." That is the second branch: fix the CES you want, then solve backwards for the distribution of firm-level AI effectiveness that supports it. The result is therefore 'there exists a distribution under which the aggregate is CES', not 'this technology aggregates to CES'. Worse for the paper's purposes, the aggregation mechanism is Houthakker-Levhari composition across Leontief firms, as Section 6.1 states plainly: "No individual firm in our model substitutes AI management labor for manual labor... Aggregate substitution comes instead from composition." Any Leontief micro technology with a suitable efficiency distribution aggregates this way; chaining plays no role in the derivation. Section 6.1 concedes the point: "The organizational content carries over as well, but only in the parameters," and its footnote lists the further conditions -- "capital productivity is common across firms, every firm organizes identically, and realized effective AI quality is the single dimension along which firms differ." With every firm organizing identically, there is no cross-firm variation in chaining at all.
why_it_matters: This is one of five sentences in the abstract and the paper's entire claim to macro relevance. Presented as stated, it invites the reader to think the sequential/chaining technology *generates* aggregate CES; it does not. A macro-literate referee who reads Appendix B will conclude the paper is claiming credit for Houthakker (1955) and Levhari (1968), both of which are cited in Section 6.1 but not in a way that makes clear they are doing all the work. It is also the clearest instance of the 'is this one paper or three?' problem: Appendix B is 295 lines and 30+ pages of the online appendix on a result orthogonal to the paper's thesis.
already_addressed: Section 6.1 is unusually candid: it names the Houthakker-Levhari mechanism, states that no firm substitutes, lists the extra assumptions in a footnote, and says the organizational content survives "only in the parameters." But the abstract does not carry any of these qualifications, and the body never states that the CES form does not depend on chaining. There is no counterexample or discussion showing what would break without the sequential technology -- because nothing would.
fix: Rewrite the abstract sentence to what Appendix B proves: 'we characterize the distribution of firm-level AI effectiveness under which this technology aggregates to a CES production function, and show how the chaining structure enters its parameters.' Then, to make the section a contribution rather than a representation exercise, deliver the object only this model can: show how $\theta_A$, $\theta_M$ and $\rho$ depend on the *arrangement* of steps -- specifically, take two economies with identical step-level exposure distributions but different autocorrelation of $d_i$ along workflows, and show they map to different CES parameters. Section 6.1 asserts exactly this ("two economies whose production steps are identically exposed to AI, differing only in how those steps are arranged... reach the same functional form... but with different weights") without proving it. Proving it would give the paper a genuine micro-to-macro contribution and would justify the fragmentation index at the aggregate level. Alternatively, cut Appendix B to a short remark and remove the claim from the abstract.

title: Section 5 carries half the title and delivers no proposition, a sign-indeterminate comparative static, and no test
location: 5_longrun.tex (whole section, esp. eq (7)-(9), l.51, l.228-236); 7_empirics.tex l.2-5; 0_main.tex l.72
claim: 'Redefining Work' is the second clause of the title and the abstract's fourth sentence embeds "this chaining problem in the firm's longer-run redesign of jobs around AI." Section 5 contains no proposition, lemma, corollary, or formal result -- `grep` for theorem environments in 5_longrun.tex returns nothing. Its content is: a wage-bill functional form, a geometric picture, and a three-task numerical example. The one substantive comparative static is stated and then withdrawn within eight lines: AI "strips out the skills the automated steps used to demand... making jobs that contain more tasks cheaper to sustain" (l.228), immediately followed by "Were that channel active, it would push the other way, toward narrower jobs and more specialization," and concluding "The net effect of AI on job breadth is therefore an empirical question our framework poses rather than settles" (l.236). Section 7 then declines to test it: "not enough time has passed since the AI tools became widely available for such reorganization to have worked its way into the data" (7_empirics.tex l.5). Meanwhile the assumption doing the work, $\text{WageBill}_j = (\sum_b \skillcost{b})(\handofftime{}(J_j) + \sum_b \timecost{b})$ -- the worker is paid for every skill the job demands over the job's whole duration -- is asserted rather than derived: "Rather than formalizing such a wage model here, we impose this as an assumption" (l.51). This multiplicative form is what makes the specialization trade-off bite, and it is strong: it implies a worker's wage rises with the *breadth* of their job even holding hours and output fixed, with no labor-supply or matching side.
why_it_matters: Stripped of Section 5, the paper is a short-run cost-minimization exercise, and the title, abstract, and framing all over-promise. As it stands, Section 5 answers the paper's own most interesting question -- does AI make jobs broader or narrower? -- with 'we cannot say'. Relative to Becker-Murphy (1992) and Garicano (2000), both cited in Section 2 without any statement of marginal contribution, Section 5's addition is a position-dependent hand-off cost $\handofftime{i}$, which yields a picture and an example but no result. A ReStud referee will ask what Section 5 buys that Becker-Murphy did not already have.
already_addressed: Section 6.2's Proposition 4 gives a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation DP for the long-run problem, so the problem is computationally tractable -- but a PTAS is not an economic result. Appendix B derives a fuller wage formulation, but for the aggregation exercise, not to justify eq (8). The section is honest about the sign ambiguity and about not testing it; the issue is that honesty does not substitute for a result.
fix: Deliver one theorem. The natural one is available and would be genuinely new: parameterize hand-off costs as $\handofftime{i} = \lambda \cdot \bar{h}_i$ with $\lambda$ the share of coordination work AI cannot absorb, and prove how optimal job breadth $p^*$ moves in $(\alpha, \lambda)$ jointly -- e.g. that $p^*$ is non-increasing in $\alpha$ for fixed $\lambda$ (chaining consolidates jobs) and non-decreasing as $\lambda$ falls (cheaper hand-offs fragment them), so the sign of AI's net effect on job breadth is governed by a single ratio of elasticities that the paper can then name and, in principle, measure. That converts "an empirical question our framework poses rather than settles" into a sufficient statistic -- which is the kind of output that makes a long-run section worth its pages. Also derive eq (8) from a short human-capital-investment problem rather than asserting it, since the multiplicative form is what generates every long-run conclusion.

title: The formal content is an EC paper: four propositions comprising one local example, one constant-factor approximation, and two dynamic programs, with no equilibrium, no welfare, and no comparative static on the wages and labor demand the paper says it changes
location: 0_main.tex (thanks footnote, ACM EC'26); 4_implications.tex Props 1-2; 6_extensions.tex Props 3-4; 1_introduction.tex l.107
claim: The paper's complete formal inventory is four propositions: Proposition 1 (local, proved by three numerical configurations plus continuity), Proposition 2 ($\tfrac18 OPT \le FI \le \tfrac54 OPT$), Proposition 3 ($O(m^2)$ DP), Proposition 4 ($O(m^2\epsilon^{-2}\log^2(mB))$ PTAS). Three of the four are computer-science results, and the vocabulary matches -- a 'prophet' with foresight motivating the fragmentation index (Sec 4.2), a greedy algorithm with an approximation guarantee, rounding costs to powers of $(1+\epsilon)$. The acknowledgments confirm the venue history: ACM EC'26. Against that, the paper repeatedly promises labor-market objects it never produces. The introduction says reorganization at a threshold shifts "labor demand and wages" (l.107); there is no wage in the short-run model (it is normalized to 1), no labor supply anywhere, no equilibrium, no welfare statement, and no comparative static of any wage or employment quantity with respect to $\alpha$. The only place wages appear is Section 5, which produces no result (see previous finding), and Appendix B, where they are inputs to a representation exercise.
why_it_matters: This is the 'one paper or several' question, and the answer is that the theory is a computational-mechanism paper, the empirics are an applied-micro paper, and the labor-economics framing belongs to neither. ReStud's theory bar asks for equilibrium objects, welfare, or comparative statics; approximation guarantees and PTAS results are valued at EC and largely discounted at a general-interest economics journal. An editor deciding whether to send this out will weigh four propositions, of which the two clean ones are algorithms, against a 45-page body and 77-page appendix.
already_addressed: Section 6 is explicitly framed as extensions and defers detail to the appendix, which is the right instinct. But moving the algorithms to Section 6 does not change the fact that they are the only fully general results in the paper. Nothing in the paper produces an equilibrium wage or an employment quantity.
fix: Close the model on the labor side for at least one exercise. Two workers types already exist in Appendix B (manual labor and AI management labor) with base wages $w_M, w_A$; put them in a simple free-entry or fixed-supply equilibrium, and derive how $w_A/w_M$ and the employment shares move as $\alpha$ crosses a reorganization threshold. The chaining mechanism has a sharp prediction here that no existing task model delivers: at a threshold the firm converts a run of manual steps into automated ones and simultaneously drops the skill requirement $\manualSkill{i}$ for those steps, so the skill premium should fall discontinuously at exactly the point where measured productivity gains accelerate. That is a labor-economics result, it is distinctive to this model, and it would reframe the paper as an economics paper with computational appendices rather than the reverse. Relegate Propositions 3-4 to the appendix entirely.

title: The closest antecedents are not cited, so the claimed novelty is asserted rather than established
claim: Section 2 positions the paper against Acemoglu-Restrepo task models, Kremer's O-ring, Milgrom-Roberts complementarities, Becker-Murphy/Garicano, and Bresnahan et al. It does not cite the literature on *sequential production with stage-specific failure*, which is where this model actually lives. Checked against `rubin.bib`: no Costinot, Vogel and Wang, 'An Elementary Theory of Global Supply Chains' (ReStud 2013) -- sequential production in which each stage fails with a stage-specific probability, a failure destroys all value added upstream, and the optimal assignment of heterogeneous workers to positions along the chain follows; no Kremer and Maskin; no Sobel; no Dixit and Grossman (1982) on multistage production; no Grossman and Rossi-Hansberg offshoring with sequential tasks; no Boehm and Oberfield; no Baldwin and Clark on modularity. Also absent is the operations-research literature on optimal inspection-station allocation in serial production lines (Lindsay and Bishop 1964; White 1969; Ballou and Pazer), where the problem of choosing where along a sequence to place costly inspections given stage-specific defect rates is solved by exactly the recursion in eq (14). The paper's positioning claims ("We depart from this literature by modeling production as a sequence of technologically interdependent steps"; "We provide a micro-foundation for these complementarities through the lens of the O-ring theory") are therefore made against a literature that excludes the papers doing the same thing.
why_it_matters: Costinot-Vogel-Wang is in ReStud and is one keyword search away from the handling editor. It shares the sequential structure, the multiplicative survival probabilities $\prod q_i$, and the resulting positional assignment of factors; what this paper adds on top is the fixed verification cost. That may well be a real addition, but the paper never says so, because it never names the paper it is adding to. Similarly, if a referee recognizes eq (14) as the inspection-allocation DP, the computational contribution (Proposition 3) evaporates. Uncited nearest neighbours are the fastest route to a referee concluding the authors do not know where their paper sits.
already_addressed: Section 2 does engage Kremer (1993) and \citet{gans2026oring}, and correctly distinguishes gans2026oring's mechanism ("time/attention reallocation rather than workflow adjacency"). It also handles \citet{trammell2026workflows} and \citet{farboodi2026data} in a footnote, distinguishing learning-based linkage from ordering-based linkage. So the paper is careful about contemporaneous AI work. The gap is the older sequential-production and operations literatures, which are absent entirely rather than partially addressed.
fix: Add a paragraph to Section 2 on sequential production with failure, and state the marginal contribution in one sentence each: relative to Costinot-Vogel-Wang, that model's positional assignment is driven by the asymmetry of downstream value destruction, whereas here it is driven by verification being a fixed cost of a contiguous block -- and crucially, this paper's automated mode has *no* human cost, which CVW has no counterpart to. Relative to the inspection-allocation literature, the difference is that the placement of a verification checkpoint also determines the skill content of a job and hence its wage (Section 5), which no OR treatment considers. Making both of these explicit strengthens the paper rather than weakening it: it converts a vague 'we depart from the task literature' into a precise statement of what is new, which is exactly what the editor's lens is looking for.
